title: How Did Sweden’s Extreme Prohibitionist Policies Work Out?

content_html_sanitized:
Most people think of Sweden as a very socially liberal country, and in most respects it certainly is. However, its “drugs” policies have been extremely Prohibitionist, especially including cannabis.

 

“Cannabis in Sweden is illegal for all purposes. It is illegal for recreational purposes, for most medical purposes and possession of even small amounts of cannabis is a criminal offence. Consequently, limited medical usage of cannabis-based drugs is only allowed for specific conditions.”

 

The rest of Sweden’s drug war is off-topic for MarijuanaNews, but they were and are pretty much in line with US policies.

See Drug policy of Sweden

 

I remember about twenty years ago when a group of Swedish journalists came to the Cannabis Cup in Amsterdam. The poor dears were simply incredulous. They really needed some medical cannabis.

 

In the meantime, two social experiments have been running in two otherwise fairly similar countries for decades.

 

The Dutch probably have a more challenging social environment. Amsterdam is a very international city and its airport is the gateway to Europe. Rotterdam is the largest port in Europe. Stockholm is tucked away in a corner of Northern Europe.

 

Well, Sweden certainly has a lower rate of per capita cannabis use, 3.2%, while the Dutch rate is roughly three times higher at  9.9 percent, in fifth place in Europe. (The highest is Spain with 12.%)

From Prevalence of cannabis use in the last year in Europe as of 2024, by country

 

However, the rate of fatal drug overdoses per capita (see graph) should be of greater concern.

 

The rate for Sweden is 82 per million, while for The Netherlands it is only 19 per million. One of the lowest in Europe. So which is the better social policy? One that makes cannabis difficult to get even for medical use, or one that has a fatal drug overdose rate that is 75% lower?
